The race falls back to data.exit.invalidation for its stock stop, so it renders in states the immediate stop-cost gate does not — a failed structural sub-fetch leaves this card pointing a reader at a row that is nowhere on the page. */} Priced at each barrier's own median day, so time decay is included. {stopCostShown ? Its risk leg is the premium minus what the contract would still be worth at the stock stop, which depends on strike, spot, time and IV independently — so it genuinely differs between contracts. baseline_contract.contract: Positive live-first anchors; directional invalidation bounds; touched/global effective premium; entry .25–3× bounds.

baseline_source.excerpt:
//  bounds. The mid falls back to the plan's own entry limit, so a card with
  //  no live and no contract mid still bounds Entry limit and Premium stop;
  //  only a card with none of the three degrades to `{min: 0.01}`.
  const firstPositive = (...xs: (number | null | undefined)[]) =>
    xs.find((x): x is number => x != null && Number.isFinite(x) && x > 0) ?? 0;
  const anchorStockPrice = firstPositive(liveStockPrice, arithmeticLiveStockPrice, data.price);
  const anchorMid = firstPositive(liveMid, data.contractDetails?.mid, data.entry.limit);

  /** Bounds for the Invalidation field, which is now load-bearing: it is what
   *  `buildPaperPosition` stores as `PortfolioPosition.stop`, and
   *  `alertEngine` compares that directly against the live UNDERLYING price.
   *  Round 5 bounded the Premium stop field for exactly this reason and the
   *  field that became the position's stop was left at `min={0.01}` with no
   *  `max` and no directional check at all.
   *
   *  Two failures, both a single mistyped digit away on a $145 stock:
   *
   *    "1400" instead of "140" — `referencePrice <= stop` is true on the very
   *    first 30s scan, so the position raises a Critical STOP_REACHED the
   *    moment it is created, with Gmail and Telegram behind it.
   *
   *    "14" instead of "140" — worse, because it is SILENT: the send gate
   *    (`checkInvalidation`) only requires a positive number, so the trade
   *    goes out with a stop the underlying will never reach and the user
   *    believes they are protected.
   *
   *  DIRECTIONAL, because "outside the bounds" is not symmetric: a bullish
   *  stop sits below the price and a bearish stop above it, and a stop on the
   *  wrong SIDE is the same silent failure as "14" — it can never fire. The
   *  window is deliberately wide (a 50% adverse move) so it rejects mistyped
   *  digits, not merely wide stops.
   *
   *  REJECTS rather than clamps, matching the Premium stop field and the
   *  Portfolio drawer. Round 8 reversed round 5's clamp choice for both: a
   *  clamp does not refuse a fat-finger, it renames it -- "1400" became
   *  $143.55, 1% below spot, stored as the position's stop and firing Critical
   *  on the first ordinary wiggle while the user believed the stop was 7%
   *  away. Out of range, the field shows the previous value back.
   *
   *  ROUND 9 -- this doc block and the premium-stop one below it were both
   *  ORPHANED, stacked above each other and attached to `round2`, which is why
   *  both drifted into asserting the opposite of their code without anything
   *  pointing at them. Reattached; keep them on the const they describe. */
  const invalidationBounds = useMemo(() => {
    // NO ANCHOR, NO DIRECTIONAL CHECK -- and that residual is stated rather
    // than hidden. With no usable stock price there is nothing to compare a
    // stop against, so this degrades to the old "must be positive". Round 8
    // flagged the same fallback on `premiumStopBounds`; there the reject-rather-
    // than-clamp policy closes the dangerous half of it (typing 0 to mean "no
    // override" no longer commits $0.01 as a deliberate 0.19% stop), but a
    // wrong-SIDE stop on an anchorless card is still accepted. A card with no
    // price is not one an order should be placed from in the first place.
    if (!(anchorStockPrice > 0)) return { min: 0.01, max: undefined as number | undefined };
    return data.direction === 'Bearish'
      ? { min: Math.max(0.01, round2(anchorStockPrice * 1.01)), max: round2(anchorStockPrice * 1.50) }
      : { min: Math.max(0.01, round2(anchorStockPrice * 0.50)), max: Math.max(0.01, round2(anchorStockPrice * 0.99)) };
  }, [anchorStockPrice, data.direction]);

  /** Bounds for the per-position premium-stop DOLLAR field.
   *
   *  The field used to be `min={0.01}` with no max, and 0.01 is not a bound so
   *  much as an invitation: `parseFloat("0")` is 0, not NaN, so typing 0 -- the
   *  natural way to say "no override, use the global" -- clamped to $0.01,
   *  differed from the seed, and therefore counted as a deliberate edit. On a
   *  $5.20 mid the server stored 0.01/5.20 = 0.19%, putting the PREMIUM_STOP
   *  threshold at $5.19 and raising a Critical alert on the first cent of
   *  adverse move. (It also used to shrink the auto-trader's daily-loss count
   *  ~3000x; since A6 that gate counts the full premium and ignores the
   *  declared stop.)
   *
   *  10%-99% OF THE MID, because that is the range the app already considers a
   *  stop: the GLOBAL premium stop is bounded `ge=0.10, le=0.99` (le=1.0 before P2-02)
   *  (routers/risk_settings.py), and the server rejects a per-position ratio at
   *  or above 1. Deriving the dollar bounds from the mid keeps the card and
   *  those two rules from disagreeing, instead of hard-coding a second opinion.
   *  The two numbers themselves now live in `premiumStop.ts`, because the
   *  Portfolio drawer edits the same quantity as a PERCENT and used to accept
   *  a band this field refuses (round 12 finding 13) -- and so does the
   *  mid-to-dollar conversion, which has to round INWARD or this field's own
   *  boundary values fall outside the band the drawer enforces. See
   *  `premiumStopDollarBounds`.
   *
   *  There IS a way back to inheriting: round 7 added `revert()`, reached by
   *  clearing the input, with a tooltip on the field saying so -- the same
   *  gesture the Portfolio drawer uses. This block used to deny that ("the
   *  card has no equivalent"), which was true when it was written and false
   *  from round 7 on. A card-level indicator of WHICH fields are pinned is
   *  still the separate approved EDITED-FLAG build. */
  const premiumStopBounds = useMemo(() => {
    if (!(anchorMid > 0)) return { min: 0.01, max: undefined as number | undefined };
    return premiumStopDollarBounds(anchorMid);
  }, [anchorMid]);

  /** P2-24 (R1-12, R2-12) -- at a mid of $0.01 the band collapses to one
   *  penny, which is 100% of the mid and produces no stop. The row is then
   *  read-only. Only for a POSITIVE anchor whose band yields no stop: with no
   *  anchor at all the field stays editable as before. */
  const premiumStopReadOnly = anchorMid > 0
    && premiumStopBounds.max != null
    && premiumStopPctFromDollars(premiumStopBounds.max, anchorMid) === undefined;

  /** P2-19 (R1-14, R2-11) -- what the untouched Premium stop row SHOWS.
   *
   *  The seed is `round(scan_mid x global, 2)` from the scan, which after a
   *  reload can be days old: a $5.20 scan mid showed a $3.12 stop against a
   *  live $1.00 mid. Untouched and with a live mid, the row shows the global
   *  applied to the live mid, labelled "(global N%)". A touched field, or no
   *  live mid, shows the overlay as before.
   *
   *  DISPLAY ONLY -- it feeds the Premium stop row and nothing else. The send
   *  paths read the tracked touched flag and are unchanged (untouched sends
   *  null). The ladder's R:R (EditableTargetRow) stays on
   *  `overlay.premiumStop`, because its reward leg is on the scan basis (code
   *  round 1, C1-1). The barrier race's snapshot and `raceBarriersMoved` stay
   *  on `overlay.premiumStop` too, so a live mid arriving does not clear a
   *  finished race -- the residual being that the race's premium barrier is
   *  the scan-seeded dollar until the field is touched.
   *
   *  A bare focus-and-blur writes nothing even when this value CHANGES while
   *  the field is open (the one-shot live quote landing mid-edit): EditableKV
   *  commits only after a keystroke (its `typedRef`), not by comparing the
   *  draft with the current value (code round 1, C1-2). */
  const premiumStopTouched = touchedRef.current.premiumStop;
  const showsGlobalOnLiveMid = !premiumStopTouched && liveMid != null && liveMid > 0;
  const effectivePremiumStop = showsGlobalOnLiveMid
    ? Math.round((liveMid as number) * globalPremiumStopPct * 100) / 100
    : overlay.premiumStop;

  /** Bounds for the Entry limit — the field this branch made into the order's
   *  `limit_price`.
   *
   *  Round 8 called this the one CRITICAL of its round, and correctly: of the
   *  three fields threaded here it is the only one whose fat-finger is an
   *  EXECUTION error rather than an alerting one. Invalidation was bounded in
   *  round 7 and Premium stop in round 5; this one shipped with `min={0.01}`
   *  and no max. On a $2.50 mid, "25.0" typed for "2.50" put
   *  `limit_price: 25.0` on a BUY/OPEN order with nothing between it and the
   *  broker: `checkTradeRisk` and the capital-at-risk row both size off
   *  `contractDetails.mid`, not off the limit. On a wide options book a
   *  marketable buy limit an order of magnitude above the ask is a real fill.
   *  (Round 8 also noted the backend's `limit_price` was an unvalidated
   *  `Optional[float]`; round 9 bounded it `gt=0` on all three order schemas,
   *  so a non-positive limit is now refused server-side too. Magnitude is
   *  still only checked here, where the live mid is known.)
   *
   *  Wider than the other two, deliberately: paying up through the ask is a
   *  legitimate thing to do with a limit order, so this has to admit real
   *  intent while rejecting a misplaced decimal point. 3x catches the missing
   *  decimal (10x) with room to spare; 0.25x catches it in the other
   *  direction. */
  const entryLimitBounds = useMemo(() => {
    if (!(anchorMid > 0)) return { min: 0.01, max: undefined as number | undefined };
    return {
      min: Math.max(0.01, round2(anchorMid * 0.25)),
      max: Math.max(0.02, round2(anchorMid * 3)),
    };

baseline_source.excerpt:
def compute_stop_cost(
    *,
    stop_price:     float,
    stock_price:    float,
    strike:         float,
    dte:            int,
    premium:        float,
    is_call:        bool,
    iv_pct:         Optional[float] = None,
    horizon_preset: Optional[str] = None,
    cfg:            Optional[dict] = None,
) -> Optional[StopCost]:
    """Price the contract at `stop_price` and grade the loss against premium.

    `iv_pct` is ABSOLUTE implied volatility in PERCENT (0-100), the same unit
    and the same field as `ContractDetails.iv` / `ContractQuoteResponse.iv`,
    NOT the decimal Black-Scholes takes. None means "solve it from the mid".

    Returns None — the card's third state, "not computed", which must never
    render as a silent PASS — when the arithmetic has no honest answer:

    * any non-finite input, or a non-positive price/strike/premium;
    * a premium under a cent (MIN_PREMIUM);
    * `dte < 1`: `bs_price` returns 0.0 for T <= 0, which would report every
      expiring contract as a 100% loss at any stop — including one that is
      deep in the money at that stop and worth its intrinsic value;
    * the IV could not be backed out of the mid. `_compute_iv_bs` refuses a
      mid at or under intrinsic (an arbitrage-violating quote), which is the
      case both solvers otherwise answer with a confidently wrong sigma.

    `fraction` is clamped to [0, 1]: a caller-supplied `iv_pct` need not
    reproduce the contract's own mid, so BS at the stop can legitimately come
    back above the premium (a negative loss) on an IV that disagrees with the
    quote. `value_at_stop` and `loss_dollar` are reported unclamped — they are
    the printed inputs, and hiding that disagreement would be hiding the one
    signal that the supplied IV and the quote do not describe the same
    contract.
    """
    values = (stop_price, stock_price, strike, premium)
    if not all(isinstance(v, (int, float)) and math.isfinite(v) for v in values):
        return None
    if stop_price <= 0 or stock_price <= 0 or strike <= 0:
        return None
    if premium < MIN_PREMIUM:
        return None
    if dte < 1:
        return None

    if iv_pct is None:
        iv_dec = _compute_iv_bs(
            mid=premium, S=stock_price, K=strike, dte=dte,
            is_call=is_call, r=RISK_FREE_RATE,
        )
    else:
        if not math.isfinite(iv_pct) or iv_pct <= 0:
            return None
        iv_dec = iv_pct / 100.0
    if iv_dec is None or iv_dec <= 0:
        return None

    raw_value = bs_price(stop_price, strike, dte / 365.0, RISK_FREE_RATE, iv_dec, is_call)
    value_at_stop = round(raw_value, 2)
    # THE PREMIUM IS QUANTIZED BEFORE THE SUBTRACTION, not after. The card
    # prints all three figures to the cent and Kenneth checks the line by
    # subtracting the two he can see, so the only version that survives a hand
    # check is the one those two numbers actually produce. Rounding
    # `premium - value_at_stop` from a RAW premium instead lets the printed
    # premium and the printed loss disagree by a cent whenever the mid sits on
    # a half-cent -- an ordinary quote, since a mid is (bid + ask) / 2.
    # Quantized first, `premium_c - value_at_stop` is exact to the cent by
    # construction and the round() below only clears binary dust.
    #
    # Guarded above by `premium < MIN_PREMIUM` on the RAW value, so this cannot
    # be zero: 0.0099 is refused before it could round up to 0.01.
    premium_c = round(premium, 2)
    loss_dollar = round(premium_c - value_at_stop, 2)
    fraction = round(min(max(loss_dollar / premium_c, 0.0), 1.0), 2)

    pass_max = pass_max_fraction_for(horizon_preset, cfg)
    # Epsilon so a fraction sitting exactly ON the line lands on CAUTION
    # rather than on whichever side binary representation puts it.
    status: Literal["PASS", "CAUTION"] = "CAUTION" if fraction + 1e-9 >= pass_max else "PASS"

    return StopCost(
        loss_dollar=loss_dollar,
        value_at_stop=value_at_stop,
        fraction=fraction,
        status=status,
        pass_max_fraction=pass_max,
        premium=premium_c,
        stop_price=stop_price,
    )

def _default_reprice_years(expiry_years: float) -> float:
    return max(expiry_years * 0.5, 7 / 365)


def estimate_rr(
    stock_price: float,
    target_price: float,
    invalidation_price: float,   # kept for call-site symmetry; risk_fraction supplies the independently priced stock-stop loss
    strike: float,
    expiry_years: float,
    current_premium: float,
    is_call: bool,
    r: float = 0.05,
    heston_params: HestonParams | None = None,
    sigma_fallback: float = 0.25,
    premium_stop_pct: float = 0.60,   # fraction of premium at risk (stop-loss basis)
    risk_fraction: float | None = None,
    reprice_years: float | None = None,   # remaining_years_at_barrier(...); None = historical half-life
    protective_stop_order: bool = False,
) -> RrResult:
    """Reward/risk of buying the contract at current_premium and selling it
    when the stock reaches target_price.

    protective_stop_order (TRADING-REVIEW-PHASE-C-RR, review M7, decision D5):
    no protective option order is ever placed -- the premium stop is an alert
    level (services/premium_stop.py) and sizing already assumes the whole
    premium can be lost. So by default (False, every caller today) the risk leg
    is the FULL premium and risk_basis is "full_premium". True restores the
    premium-stop / captured stock-stop basis (resolved_risk_dollars) unchanged,
    for the day a real protective order exists.
    """
    if captured_stock_risk(current_premium, risk_fraction) is not None:
        current_premium = round(current_premium, 2)
    model_used: RrModel
    heston_ok = False
    dte_at_target = reprice_years if reprice_years is not None else _default_reprice_years(expiry_years)

    if heston_params is not None:
        try:
            detail = heston_price_detail(target_price, strike, dte_at_target, r, heston_params, is_call)
            # fell_back: the integration failed and the price is Black-Scholes
            # at sqrt(v0), not Heston -- treat it exactly like a failed Heston
            # price so it is never labelled "Heston repriced" (DECISION-23 H-1).
            heston_exit_premium = 0.0 if detail.fell_back else detail.price
        except Exception:
            heston_exit_premium = 0.0
        heston_ok = math.isfinite(heston_exit_premium) and heston_exit_premium > 0

    if heston_ok:
        exit_premium = heston_exit_premium
        model_used = "Heston repriced"
    else:
        sigma = _derive_fallback_sigma(current_premium, stock_price, strike, expiry_years, r, is_call, sigma_fallback)
        exit_premium, used_bs_reprice = _bs_reprice_or_delta_approx(
            target_price, stock_price, strike, dte_at_target, r, sigma, is_call, current_premium,
        )
        model_used = "BS repriced (IV-derived)" if used_bs_reprice else "Delta approximation"

baseline_source.excerpt:
def resolve_reprice_days(
    preset: Optional[str],
    hold_min: Optional[float],
    hold_max: Optional[float],
    dte: float,
    sim_median: Optional[float],
    cfg: Optional[dict] = None,
) -> float:
    """Days ahead to reprice at, for one barrier.

    ``sim_median`` is the simulation's own conditional median days to THAT
    barrier (``None`` when no path reached it). ``dte`` is calendar days to
    expiry. Returns a number of days ELAPSED until the barrier — never a time
    to expiry; see the module docstring and ``remaining_years_at_barrier``.

    Bounds, precisely:

    * A FALLBACK value is clamped to ``[min_days, max_fraction_of_dte * dte]``,
      the ceiling winning when the two conflict — a holding-period table knows
      nothing about this contract's expiry.
    * A usable ``sim_median`` is floored at ``min_days`` and capped half a day
      short of expiry, but ``max_fraction_of_dte`` NEVER applies to it: it
      cannot exceed the contract's life by construction, and overriding a
      measured value with an arbitrary fraction is a worse answer, not a safer
      one. The half-day cap is not that fraction — it only stops a median that
      lands exactly ON expiry from leaving zero life to price with.

    So ``resolve_reprice_days("Swing", None, None, dte=1, sim_median=1.0)`` is
    0.5, and ``(..., dte=30, sim_median=0.1)`` is 1.0. Both bounds do reach the
    simulated median; only the DTE fraction does not.
    """
    cfg = cfg if cfg is not None else load_reprice_horizon_cfg()
    fallback = cfg.get("fallback_days", {}) or {}
    clamp = cfg.get("clamp", {}) or {}
    min_days = float(clamp.get("min_days", 1))
    max_fraction = float(clamp.get("max_fraction_of_dte", 0.75))

    if cfg.get("source", "simulation_median") == "simulation_median" and _usable(sim_median):
        # Returned as observed, NOT clamped to max_fraction_of_dte. See the
        # module docstring: that ceiling exists to protect the FALLBACK from a
        # holding-period table that knows nothing about this contract's expiry,
        # and overriding a measurement with an arbitrary fraction of DTE is a
        # worse answer rather than a safer one.
        #
        # It IS capped just short of expiry, though. A simulated median cannot
        # exceed the contract's life, but it can EQUAL it: the median is a day
        # index plus one, so it ranges 1..dte, and at dte exactly the remaining
        # life collapses to remaining_years_at_barrier's floor and every level
        # prices at intrinsic value only — the outcome the ceiling exists to
        # prevent, arrived at from the other direction. Reachable whenever the
        # simulated median lands on the final day — always the case at dte=1,
        # where the median is exactly 1.0.
        #
        # THE CEILING IS APPLIED LAST, so it wins when it conflicts with the
        # min_days floor — the same precedence the fallback branch below uses,
        # and for the same reason. Written the other way round (`max(min_days,
        # min(median, dte - 0.5))`) the floor won at dte=1, which is where a
        # simulated median is ALWAYS exactly 1.0, so the cap silently did
        # nothing on precisely the contracts it mattered most for: a 1-DTE
        # stop priced at zero remaining life makes the risk leg the whole
        # premium and collapses rr_stock_stop to exactly the typed target
        # percentage — indistinguishable from the greyed constant it is printed
        # beside, on a card whose point is that the two differ.
        return min(max(min_days, float(sim_median)), _latest_barrier_day(dte))

    days = _fallback_days(preset, hold_min, hold_max, fallback, cfg)

    # Clamp. The DTE ceiling only applies when we actually know the DTE — a
    # non-positive or non-finite dte means "unknown", and silently collapsing
    # to min_days there would be a worse answer than the preset's own.
    #
    # The ceiling is applied LAST, so it wins when it conflicts with the floor.
    # On a 1-DTE contract 0.75 x dte is 0.75 of a day and min_days is 1: letting
    # the floor win there puts the barrier exactly AT expiry, leaving zero
    # remaining life and pricing every level at intrinsic value only — the very
    # thing max_fraction_of_dte exists to prevent.
    days = max(min_days, days)
    if dte is not None and _usable(dte) and dte > 0:
        days = min(days, max_fraction * float(dte))
    return days


def _latest_barrier_day(dte: float) -> float:
    """The latest day a barrier may be said to be reached, so there is always
    some life left to price with. Returns +inf when the DTE is unknown, leaving
    the caller's other bounds to decide.

    Half a day before expiry, EXCEPT on a sub-1-day contract, where a flat
    "dte - 0.5" floored at 0.5 lands at or past expiry — 0.5 on a 0.4-day
    contract — which is the exact outcome this cap exists to prevent, reached
    from the other side. Falling back to half the remaining life keeps it
    strictly inside the contract for any positive DTE. Not reachable through
    the race today (estimate_first_passage refuses dte < 1) — see the note in
    the branch below for why Stage 1 does not reach it either. Kept so the rule
    is total, since this module is documented as its single owner."""
    if dte is None or not _usable(dte) or dte <= 0:
        return float("inf")
    latest = float(dte) - 0.5
    if latest <= 0:
        # Sub-1-day contract: half its remaining life, which is strictly inside
        # it. Taking a min() of the two instead would cap EVERY median at half
        # the DTE — reintroducing the fixed half-life this module exists to
        # replace, on every contract rather than the sub-1-day ones.
        #
        # UNREACHABLE TODAY, and kept anyway so the rule is total. The only
        # caller of _latest_barrier_day is the sim_median branch, and the only
        # way to have a sim_median is to have run the simulation, which
        # estimate_first_passage refuses below dte 1. An earlier version of this
        # comment claimed Stage 1 reached it — Stage 1 passes sim_median=None
        # and takes the fallback branch, which never calls this.
        latest = float(dte) * 0.5
    return latest


def _fallback_days(
    preset: Optional[str],
    hold_min: Optional[float],
    hold_max: Optional[float],
    fallback: dict,
    cfg: dict,
) -> float:
    """The per-preset table, or Custom's derivation from the typed range."""
    if preset == _CUSTOM:
        custom = cfg.get("custom", {}) or {}
        fraction = float(custom.get("fraction", 0.5))
        lo = float(hold_min) if _usable(hold_min) else None
        hi = float(hold_max) if _usable(hold_max) else None
        if lo is None and hi is None:
            # "Custom" with nothing typed carries no information at all.
            # Deriving from a 0-0 range would silently return 0 days (then the
            # floor, so 1) — a made-up answer dressed as a derived one. Fall
            # through to the table's own default instead.
            return float(fallback.get("Swing", 7))
        lo = lo if lo is not None else hi
        hi = hi if hi is not None else lo
        if (lo + hi) <= 0:
            # A typed 0-0 range is the same non-information as an empty one, and
            # reachable: HORIZON_PRESETS' Intraday row carries holdMin 0, so
            # zeros do arrive here. Deriving 0 days from it, then flooring to 1,
            # is the made-up-answer-dressed-as-a-derived-one this branch exists
            # to avoid.
            return float(fallback.get("Swing", 7))
        # Chosen over snapping to the nearest preset: a manual 30-35 day range
        # sits between Position and Quarterly and either snap moves the
        # repriced loss by real money. scoringHorizonForHold already sets the
        # precedent of deriving from the typed range.
        return ((lo + hi) / 2.0) * fraction

    if preset in fallback:
        return float(fallback[preset])

    # Unknown/absent preset: Swing is the app's own default horizon
    # (presetByKey falls back to HORIZON_PRESETS[1], which is Swing).
    return float(fallback.get("Swing", 7))


def remaining_years_at_barrier(
    dte: float, days_to_barrier: float, floor_years: float = 1e-6,
) -> float:
    """Time to expiry REMAINING, in years, at the moment a barrier is reached.

    ``days_to_barrier`` is what resolve_reprice_days returns: days ELAPSED from
    today until the barrier. Black-Scholes wants what is left after that, so the
    conversion is ``dte - days_to_barrier``, never ``days_to_barrier`` itself.

    THE TRAP THIS EXISTS FOR: passing elapsed days into bs_price's ``T`` inverts
    theta. A stop hit on day 2 of a 60-day contract would be priced as if two
    days of life remained (worth ~nothing, so the risk leg swallows the whole
    premium), while a stop hit on day 45 would be priced as if 45 days remained
    (worth MORE than the earlier one). Both wrong, and wrong in the direction
    that overstates risk on exactly the fast stop-outs that matter most.

    Floors at ``floor_years`` rather than returning zero or negative: bs_price
    returns 0.0 for T <= 0, which is intrinsic value, and that is the right
    answer at expiry — but the floor keeps the call in the pricing branch so a
    barrier clamped to the very end of the contract still prices continuously.
    """
    if not _usable(dte) or not _usable(days_to_barrier):
        return floor_years
    return max((float(dte) - float(days_to_barrier)) / 365.0, floor_years)


def _usable(x: Optional[float]) -> bool:
    """Finite and numeric. math.isfinite rather than an identity check against
    the infinities: it also rejects NaN (which compares equal to nothing,
    itself included) and accepts numpy scalars, which arrive here from the
    simulation's own medians."""
    if x is None:
        return False
    try:
        return math.isfinite(float(x))
